findings.checklist_item: - [ ] State the default constraints for `no_file_impact_reason` in the plan (e.g., 'any non-empty string up to N characters; no structured format required') so the S1 validation and S4 rubric fixture implementations share a consistent expectation.
evidence: 'Declaring `none` without `no_file_impact_reason` is rejected (checked: S1 validation test)'
'An accepted `no_file_impact_reason` persists in reduced ticket state (checked: S1 round-trip test)'
ABSENCE: no mention of minimum length, format requirements, or structured vs. free-text for the reason field
findings.finding: The `no_file_impact_reason` field is declared 'required' for the `none` state, but the plan specifies no constraints on what constitutes a valid reason — no minimum length, no format (free-text vs structured), no vocabulary restriction. An executor implementing S1 validation must infer these constraints.
findings.location: Acceptance Criteria — 'Declaring `none` without `no_file_impact_reason` is rejected (checked: S1 validation test)' and S1 child description
scenarios: An executor implementing S1 validation might accept a single-space string as a valid reason, or might impose arbitrary length minimums — the plan does not constrain this, making the validation boundary underdetermined.
A reviewer evaluating S1 cannot confirm the validation is correct without knowing what 'accepted' means.
findings.suggested_fix: Add to the S1 description or AC6: 'A valid `no_file_impact_reason` is any non-empty, non-whitespace-only string; no minimum length or structured format is required beyond non-emptiness.'

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Resolve the contradiction between the Approach's neutral-contribution rule and S3's 'all-declared-none container is itself scope-none' rule by picking one semantics and stating it explicitly in both the Approach and S3.
evidence: Approach: 'the child neither contributes to nor poisons a container\'s inherited drift scope'
S3: 'a container whose live children are ALL declared-none is itself scope-none'
If neutral contribution means the container accumulates nothing from its children, the container would be undeclared (empty list, no declaration), not scope-none — the opposite of S3's claim.
findings.finding: The Approach section describes declared-none children as neutral (they 'neither contribute to nor poison a container's inherited drift scope'), which would leave an all-declared-none container with an empty, *undeclared* scope — triggering whole-HEAD fallback. But S3 explicitly states 'a container whose live children are ALL declared-none is itself scope-none.' These two descriptions produce different outcomes for the all-none-children case and point the implementer in two directions.
findings.location: Approach section ('the child neither contributes to nor poisons...') vs Child decomposition S3 ('a container whose live children are ALL declared-none is itself scope-none')
scenarios: Implementer codes `_inherited_child_impact` to return neutral/empty for an all-none container (following Approach), while AC/S3 expects it to return scope-none — the unit test in AC3 would pass or fail depending on which description was followed.
findings.suggested_fix: In the Approach, add a sentence: 'When all live children of a container are declared-none and none are undeclared, the container itself inherits scope-none.' Then remove or qualify the 'neither contributes to nor poisons' phrasing to clarify it only applies to mixed containers.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Add an AC verifying that `p9_file_impact_coverage` does NOT fire for a ticket with an explicit declared-none `file_impact` (e.g., 'A declared-none ticket passes P9 lint without advisory — checked: S3 unit/integration test over `p9_file_impact_coverage` with a declared-none fixture').

findings.location: Approach section; Child decomposition S3; Acceptance Criteria (full set)
scenarios: An implementer skips the P9 suppression change, all other ACs pass, and the feature ships with declared-none tickets still receiving P9 advisories — the problem the plan set out to fix.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Add an explicit migration note to S2 clarifying whether the fingerprint encoding for `undeclared`/`paths` tickets changes on upgrade (and if so, provide an expand-contract or no-op migration strategy so existing attestations are not silently mass-invalidated on deploy).
evidence: 'The declaration is part of the material fingerprint, so flipping between the three states invalidates the attestation'
ABSENCE: no migration note, no expand-contract sequence, no statement about existing attestations on upgrade
If fingerprint computation changes even for `undeclared` tickets (e.g., by encoding the tri-state enum into the hash), all existing attestations are invalidated on deploy
findings.finding: The plan changes `material_fingerprint` computation in S2, but does not address what happens to *existing* signed attestations on deploy — specifically, whether tickets currently storing empty `file_impact` (which become `undeclared`) will have their fingerprint silently change, forcing a fleet-wide re-review of all existing attestations the moment the new code ships.
findings.location: S2 — attestation scoping; Acceptance Criteria: 'Every state transition of the tri-state changes the material fingerprint'
scenarios: On deploy, every previously-attested ticket (even ones with carefully declared `paths`) triggers forced re-review if the fingerprint encoding changes
Operators cannot roll back the code change without re-invalidating all attestations in the opposite direction
findings.suggested_fix: Ensure the `undeclared` and `paths` fingerprint encoding is byte-for-byte identical to the pre-change encoding (i.e., the tri-state field is only injected into the fingerprint when `none` is declared), and state this explicitly in S2 so reviewers and implementers know not to touch the existing hash paths.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Add an explicit rollback / back-out plan (e.g., forward-only migration with old-reader tolerates unknown fields, or a feature flag for the tri-state until S1–S3 are proven stable) covering what happens to already-written `none` events if the implementation is reverted.

Because FILE_IMPACT events will be written with the new fields once S1 ships, rolling back the code would leave the reducer unable to handle events it previously wrote, or would silently revert `none` declarations to `undeclared` with no operator visibility.
findings.location: S1 — data model + write/read surface; S2 — attestation scoping; overall plan structure
scenarios: A bug in S2 is discovered post-deploy; rolling back the code causes all `none`-declared tickets to silently revert to `undeclared` behavior (whole-HEAD invalidation), breaking user trust
If the event schema validation is strict on read (not just write), old code reading new events may crash

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Specify in S3 how the all-none determination travels from `_inherited_child_impact` to `build_manifest`: either change the return type to a discriminated union/sentinel (e.g. a named tuple or an enum-tagged result), or add an out-of-band parameter so `build_manifest` can emit the `file-scope: none` manifest line for containers.
evidence: manifest.py:274-275: `if not paths: return set()  # poison: undeclared scope on a live child → whole-HEAD fallback`
manifest.py:294: `paths.update(_inherited_child_impact(children))`
attest.py:691-714: `if deps:` branch does scoped re-hashing; `else:` branch does whole-HEAD check — both `{}` cases (poison and all-none) fall to `else`
S3 plan text: 'a container whose live children are ALL declared-none is itself scope-none' — but no mechanism for communicating this determination to `build_manifest` is specified
findings.finding: `_inherited_child_impact` returns an undiscriminated `set()` for both 'poison/undeclared child' and 'all live children are none-scoped', so `dependency_hashes` and `build_manifest` cannot distinguish the two cases and would fall through to whole-HEAD invalidation for an all-none container.
findings.location: S3 — container roll-up; manifest.py:241-278 (`_inherited_child_impact`), manifest.py:281-305 (`dependency_hashes`)
scenarios: A container with two `none`-scoped non-closed children is reviewed; the attestation should survive any commit, but `_inherited_child_impact` returns `set()` → `dependency_hashes` returns `{}` → `compute_validity` fires whole-HEAD check → attestation invalidated on the next unrelated commit.
S3's unit test over `_inherited_child_impact` may pass if it only checks the returned `set()`, but the downstream `compute_validity` behavior would still be wrong.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Explicitly add the new tri-state field (e.g. `file_impact_scope` or `no_file_impact_reason`) to the `material_fingerprint` basis dict in `pass1.py` so that every tri-state transition produces a distinct fingerprint.
evidence: pass1.py:558: `'file_impact': ctx.state.get('file_impact') or []` — the basis dict has no entry for the new tri-state field
Both `undeclared` (file_impact=[]) and `none` (file_impact=[], no_file_impact_reason='…') produce `'file_impact': []` in the basis, yielding identical SHA-256 hashes

Plan AC5: 'Every state transition of the tri-state changes the material fingerprint (checked: unit test over material_fingerprint)' — the unit test would expose this IF it hashes both states and asserts inequality

findings.location: S1 — data model; pass1.py:551-562 (`material_fingerprint`), AC: 'Every state transition of the tri-state changes the material fingerprint'
scenarios: Author sets `file_impact_scope=none` with a reason after the attestation is signed; material fingerprint is unchanged; `compute_validity` does not detect the edit; old whole-HEAD attestation remains valid, now carrying an incorrect scope claim.
findings.suggested_fix: Add `'file_impact_scope': ctx.state.get('file_impact_scope', 'undeclared')` (or the equivalent field name from S1) to the `basis` dict in `material_fingerprint`.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Verify (or specify) that the criteria-routing infrastructure supports a field-value-based deterministic trigger (e.g. `trigger_when: file_impact_scope == none`); if not, add a sub-step to S4 (or a new child) to extend the router before adding the `no-file-impact` criterion.

The existing routing infrastructure (`criteria_routing.json` + routing logic) supports suppression only by `scope`, `suppress_types`, `suppress_when`, and `require_parent_id` — there is no field-value predicate mechanism. Adding this trigger requires new routing capability not currently present, but the plan treats it as already available.
findings.location: Acceptance Criteria — 'A plan-review criterion fires on the PRESENCE of the no-file-impact assertion — and only then — and uses LLM judgment'; Child S4 — 'triggered deterministically by the presence of the assertion'

The orchestrator's deterministic routing pass includes the criterion unconditionally (or excludes it unconditionally) because the routing spec has no way to express field-value conditions, defeating the 'triggered deterministically' AC

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] S1 must specify how the new process_file_impact handles an unscoped FILE_IMPACT event written AFTER a scoped one (LWW must reset scope to 'undeclared', not inherit the prior 'none').
evidence: FILE_IMPACT uses last-writer-wins (process_file_impact replaces state on each event)
ABSENCE: plan does not mention the deployment transition window or mixed-event epoch

findings.finding: The plan does not address the dual-write window: during the deployment epoch, old writers (undeployed instances or CLI versions) still append FILE_IMPACT events without file_impact_scope. The new reader will encounter a mix of scoped and unscoped events for the same ticket, and must apply LWW (last-writer-wins) correctly, but no handling of this mixed-epoch stream is specified.
findings.location: S1 — data model + write/read surface
scenarios: Author sets scope=none via new CLI, then an old-CLI call to set-file-impact overwrites with an unscoped event — new reader must treat the latest event as undeclared, not inherit the prior scope=none.
findings.suggested_fix: Since LWW replaces the whole file_impact state on each event, derive scope from the event data alone (no prior-state inheritance). An unscoped event always yields undeclared regardless of prior events.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] S4: Specify the concrete routing hook that connects `file_impact_scope == none` (a deterministic state read) to the `no-file-impact` LLM criterion — e.g. a new entry in `_DET_OVERLAY_RULES`, a dedicated pre-pass check, or a new `applies_when` key in `criteria_routing.json` — so the routing test AC is implementable.

findings.finding: The routing mechanism for `no-file-impact` is underspecified and inconsistent with the existing overlay infrastructure. A criterion named `no-file-impact` will not be recognised as an overlay, so the orchestrator's `overlay_triggers()` / `is_overlay()` routing path cannot handle it.
